segments.text: Here are tiny glowing beads, each one far smaller than the wavelength of light.
Now look at them through a perfect microscope. Every bead has become a soft disc, wrapped in faint rings.
Push two beads closer than about 200 nanometres, and they merge into a single blob.
No lens maker can fix this. So why can't even a perfect lens make a perfect point?
First, what is an image? Think of any object as a crowd of tiny points of light.
A lens turns each point into the same small blur, called the point spread function, or PSF.
Each point stamps a copy of the PSF at its own position, scaled by its brightness. The beads glow independently, so the stamps simply add.
Adding up shifted copies like this is called a convolution. The image is the object, convolved with the PSF.
Now feed the blur a single wave, a pattern of stripes. Out comes the same wave, only fainter.
Just like propagation in episode one, waves are the eigenvectors of blurring. In the Fourier basis, convolution becomes multiplication.
Each spatial frequency kx just gets multiplied by one number: the transfer function, the Fourier transform of the PSF.
Notice how fine stripes fade much more than coarse ones.
So where does the PSF come from? Recall episode one: any light field is a sum of plane waves.
A point sends them out in every direction, each with its own kx = k sin θ. Together they fill the k-circle.
But a lens has a finite opening. It only catches waves tilted less than some largest angle.
The sine of that angle is the numerical aperture, NA. On the k-circle, the lens keeps just a cap: kx up to k times NA.
Waves with kx beyond k are evanescent: they never even leave the object. So the lens is a hole in k-space, called the pupil.
Add up only the waves that pass through this hole, and you get the PSF. Watch what happens as the aperture opens.
The cap widens, and the spot shrinks. Its bright core, the Airy disc, has a radius of 0.61 λ/NA.
And magnification can't save you: zooming in on the image only gives you a bigger blur.
In 1873, Ernst Abbe asked a sharper question: what is the finest grating a lens can image?
A grating of period d splits a plane wave into a straight beam and two first orders, tilted at sin θ = ±λ/d.
The lens must catch the straight beam and at least one first order: their interference rebuilds the stripes.
Now make the grating finer. The orders tilt further out, and once they leave the cap, the stripes are gone.
So with straight-on light, the finest period a lens can image is λ/NA.
Abbe's trick: tilt the illumination, so the straight beam enters at one edge of the cap. Now a first order fits in at the other edge.
That doubles the reach, to a finest period of λ/2NA. This is the diffraction limit.
Abbe's picture is for coherent light, like a laser, where fields add: the pupil cuts the field off sharply at k·NA.
Glowing beads are different: each emits with its own random, ever-changing phase, so intensities add, not fields.
Then the transfer function, called the OTF, is the overlap of the pupil with a shifted copy of itself.
Slide one copy across the other. The overlap shrinks smoothly, and only reaches zero at twice the coherent cutoff.
So incoherent light reaches twice as far in kx. But it isn't simply better: its contrast fades toward the cutoff.
Here's one test chart, imaged both ways. Coherent light rings at every edge; incoherent light is smooth, but its finest spokes wash out.
On a computer, imaging is the same three steps as in episode one: FFT, multiply by the OTF, inverse FFT.
So can we run it backwards? Take a blurred image with a little camera noise, and divide by the OTF.
Disaster. Wherever the OTF is tiny, the noise gets multiplied by thousands, and swamps everything.
The Wiener filter is the stable version. It divides where the signal beats the noise, and gently gives up where it doesn't.
But beyond the cutoff, the OTF is exactly zero. Those details never reached the camera, and no filter can bring them back.
Only prior knowledge or extra measurements can fill them in. And that's where computational imaging begins.
So here is the whole idea. Imaging is convolution with the PSF.
A lens only keeps directions with sin θ ≤ NA, so details finer than about λ/2NA never arrive.
One honest caveat: real lenses blur differently away from the centre, so the PSF slowly changes across the field.
And we saw that intensities add for glowing beads. But why? When does light interfere, and when doesn't it?
